title: US Clouds Host DeepSeek on 16 Providers Despite Export Push
summary: Georgetown CSET researchers find DeepSeek running on 16 US-based inference providers, including Amazon Bedrock, undermining export controls on Chinese AI.
body_markdown:
#### 💡 TL;DR


- Georgetown CSET researchers find DeepSeek available through 16 inference providers outside China, including Amazon Bedrock and major US neoclouds.
- Moonshot AI reportedly seeks 30% revenue share from Microsoft, Amazon, and Google for Kimi K3 deployments exceeding $20M in annual sales.
- Analysis argues US should release competitive open-weight models rather than tighten infrastructure controls following Commerce Department's November 16 chip-access rule.


Three Georgetown researchers have documented a striking paradox in US AI policy: while the Trump administration pushes[export controls](https://emergent.sh/news/3-u-s-ai-chip-stocks-facing-export-rules) to limit Chinese AI capabilities, American cloud infrastructure is actively distributing Chinese models. DeepSeek's latest model is now available through at least 16 inference providers headquartered outside China, including Amazon Bedrock, with Together AI, Baseten, and Fireworks all running Chinese model weights on US-chip-powered servers.


## US Cloud Dominance Enables Chinese Model Distribution


Jacob Feldgoise, Hanna Dohmen, and Sam Bresnick of Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology argue in Fortune that US cloud providers have become the primary delivery mechanism for Chinese open-weight AI models. Amazon, Microsoft, and Google collectively control more than half of the global cloud market, with a growing cohort of American neoclouds extending that dominance. Nearly all deployed data-center AI chips were designed by US firms including Nvidia, Google, AMD, and Amazon, creating an infrastructure foundation that Chinese developers now leverage for global distribution.


The analysis identifies DeepSeek as a prime example, with its latest model accessible through providers spanning multiple jurisdictions. The researchers note that Chinese models are running on US chips, and the ongoing American AI infrastructure build-out is counterintuitively helping Chinese model developers compete on the global stage.


## Moonshot AI Seeks 30% Revenue Share From Cloud Giants


Moonshot AI, the developer behind the Kimi K3 model, has reportedly requested a 30% revenue share from Microsoft, Amazon, and Google for customers exceeding $20 million in annual sales. The company requires any organization serving Kimi K3 that surpasses this revenue threshold to negotiate a revenue-sharing license, creating a direct financial link between Chinese AI developers and American cloud infrastructure.


This revenue-sharing structure represents a novel business model in the AI space, where Chinese labs capture value from US cloud providers' customer relationships rather than building their own global distribution networks. The arrangement highlights how open-weight models enable licensing flexibility that closed models cannot match.


## Commerce Department Rule Targets Remote Chip Access


The analysis comes days after the US Commerce Department issued an interim rule on November 16, 2026, aimed at closing a loophole around remote access to advanced semiconductors by Chinese firms. Officially released on November 16, 2026, the rule attempts to restrict Chinese companies from accessing US-designed AI chips through cloud infrastructure, addressing precisely the scenario the Georgetown researchers document.


The timing underscores ongoing tensions between export control policy and market realities. While regulators work to limit Chinese firms' physical access to advanced chips, those same firms have already secured broad distribution through American cloud platforms that operate on US semiconductor technology.


## Open-Weight Competition vs Infrastructure Restrictions


The CSET authors prescribe a strategic shift: rather than further tightening infrastructure access, they argue the US should field competitive open-weight models. This recommendation challenges the prevailing export-control approach, suggesting that American competitiveness depends more on model quality than on restricting Chinese access to US cloud resources.


The research sits within a broader pattern of China-AI coverage this month. Rhodium Group recently projected that top Chinese AI firms will roughly double their AI capital expenditure to $139 billion, signaling sustained investment despite US restrictions. The combination of rising Chinese capex and widespread US cloud distribution suggests that export controls alone may not achieve their intended strategic effects.


## What This Means


The Georgetown analysis reveals a fundamental tension in US AI strategy: infrastructure dominance does not automatically translate to competitive advantage when open-weight models enable rival nations to leverage that infrastructure for their own distribution. As Chinese labs continue shipping capable models and American cloud providers continue hosting them, policymakers face a choice between escalating restrictions that may prove unenforceable and competing directly through superior open-weight releases. The 30% revenue share Moonshot seeks from cloud giants suggests Chinese developers have found a profitable path through the US infrastructure ecosystem, one that export controls have not yet closed.
